title: Health Checks & Circuit Breakers
description: Learn how active and passive health checks detect failing backends, how circuit breakers prevent cascading failures, and why the bulkhead pattern saved Netflix.

segments.text: Your load balancer is only as good as its knowledge of backend health. Send traffic to a dead server and you've turned your load balancer into a load multiplier. Let's talk about how production systems detect failure before users do.

Active health checks are probes your load balancer sends periodically. Every five seconds, hit slash health on each backend. If three consecutive checks fail, mark it unhealthy and stop routing traffic. AWS ALB does exactly this. But there's a catch: your health endpoint might return 200 while your database connection pool is exhausted.

Passive health checks observe real traffic. If a backend returns five consecutive 503s from actual user requests, mark it down. No extra probe traffic, and you catch problems that synthetic checks miss. Envoy calls this outlier detection, and it's what catches those partial failures that health endpoints hide.
segments.thought_prompt: What happens if a backend is slow but not failing? How would health checks catch that?

segments.text: Now the circuit breaker. Picture a service calling a downstream dependency. If that dependency is down, every request hangs for thirty seconds waiting for a timeout. Multiply by a thousand concurrent requests and you've just exhausted your thread pool. Your healthy service is now dead too. That's a cascading failure.

A circuit breaker has three states. Closed means normal, requests flow through. When failures exceed a threshold, say fifty percent in a ten-second window, it trips to Open. All requests immediately fail fast, no waiting. After a cooldown of thirty seconds, it moves to Half-Open, letting one test request through.

Half-Open is where the magic happens. That single test request determines everything. If it succeeds, the circuit closes and traffic resumes. If it fails, back to Open for another cooldown. This gives a struggling service time to recover instead of drowning it with retries the moment it shows signs of life.

Netflix's Hystrix pioneered this pattern in Java. Every external call wrapped in a HystrixCommand with timeout, thread pool isolation, and fallback logic. When recommendations service died, the UI showed generic suggestions instead of a blank page. Hystrix is deprecated now, but its ideas live on in resilience4j.

Resilience4j is the modern successor. Lightweight, functional, composable. You chain decorators: CircuitBreaker, then RateLimiter, then Retry, then Bulkhead. Each is independent and configurable. The key improvement over Hystrix: it uses the calling thread instead of a dedicated thread pool, so you avoid the overhead.

The bulkhead pattern is borrowed from ship design. Ships have watertight compartments so a hull breach doesn't sink the whole vessel. In software, you isolate dependency calls into separate thread pools. If your payment service goes down and exhausts its pool of twenty threads, your search service's pool of fifty threads is completely unaffected.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you size the thread pool for each bulkhead? What data would you need?

segments.text: In 2012, Netflix had a cascading failure that took down their entire streaming platform. One overloaded API caused thread pool exhaustion across all services. After that, they implemented bulkheads with Hystrix for every single external call. Response: two hundred millisecond timeout, ten-thread pools, immediate fallback.

The takeaway: health checks tell you what's dead, circuit breakers protect you from what's dying, and bulkheads contain the blast radius. In production, you need all three. Fail fast, fail gracefully, fail in isolation. That's the resilience trifecta.
